title: Scarcity, systems and the next-best alternative
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Scarcity means desired uses exceed available resources, even for wealthy societies. A choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative forgone, not the sum of all rejected options. Prices, rules and institutions affect who decides what to produce, how to produce it and who receives it. A positive claim describes a testable relationship; a normative claim depends on a value judgment.
formula: Opportunity cost = value of the next-best forgone alternative
steps: A student has one free evening.
Studying yields a personal benefit valued at 40; working would earn 30; a film is valued at 20.
If the student studies, the next-best alternative is working, worth 30.
The opportunity cost is 30, not 50; whether studying is worthwhile also depends on its benefit.
trap: A monetary payment is not required for an opportunity cost to exist.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A student has one free evening. Studying yields a personal benefit valued at 40; working would earn 30; a film is valued at 20. If the student studies, the next-best alternative is working, worth 30. The opportunity cost is 30, not 50; whether studying is worthwhile also depends on its benefit. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Reading a production frontier
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A production possibilities curve shows attainable combinations when resources and technology are fixed and used efficiently. A point inside is attainable but productively inefficient; a point outside is currently unattainable. Moving along the frontier reallocates resources. A bowed-out frontier represents increasing opportunity cost as resources suited to one use move to another. More resources or better technology can shift the frontier outward.
formula: Opportunity cost of X = Y forgone / additional X
steps: An economy moves from 10 tools and 60 meals to 14 tools and 48 meals on its frontier.
The change produces four additional tools.
It gives up 12 meals.
The average opportunity cost over this interval is 12 / 4 = 3 meals per tool.
trap: Movement from inside to the frontier is fuller resource use, not necessarily growth of productive capacity.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: An economy moves from 10 tools and 60 meals to 14 tools and 48 meals on its frontier. The change produces four additional tools. It gives up 12 meals. The average opportunity cost over this interval is 12 / 4 = 3 meals per tool. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Movement from inside to the frontier is fuller resource use, not necessarily growth of productive capacity.

title: Comparative advantage and gains from exchange
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources. Comparative advantage means a lower opportunity cost. Specialization based on comparative advantage can expand consumption possibilities, even when one producer has absolute advantage in both goods. Mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the producers’ opportunity costs, with the units stated consistently. Trade does not automatically determine how the gains are shared.
formula: Mutually beneficial price: between the two opportunity costs
steps: In one day, A can make 12 loaves or 6 bowls; B can make 8 loaves or 8 bowls.
A sacrifices 2 loaves per bowl; B sacrifices 1 loaf per bowl.
B has comparative advantage in bowls; A in loaves.
At 1.5 loaves per bowl, B receives more than its cost and A pays less than its cost.
trap: Comparative advantage compares opportunity costs, not output totals alone.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: In one day, A can make 12 loaves or 6 bowls; B can make 8 loaves or 8 bowls. A sacrifices 2 loaves per bowl; B sacrifices 1 loaf per bowl. B has comparative advantage in bowls; A in loaves. At 1.5 loaves per bowl, B receives more than its cost and A pays less than its cost. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Comparative advantage compares opportunity costs, not output totals alone.
questions.explain: B, because its opportunity cost is lower.

title: Marginal choice and consumer allocation
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A rational choice compares the additional benefit with the additional cost of the next unit. Sunk costs are already incurred and cannot be recovered; they do not change the marginal comparison. With divisible goods and an interior optimum, a consumer allocates a fixed budget so marginal utility per dollar is equal across purchases. Utility is a model of preferences, not a directly comparable measure of happiness across people.
formula: Choose additional units while MB ≥ MC; interior allocation: MUx / Px = MUy / Py
steps: The next notebook yields 18 units of utility and costs 3.
The next pen yields 10 units and costs 2.
Notebook utility per dollar is 6; pen utility per dollar is 5.
At this margin, shifting some spending toward notebooks improves utility until the ratios converge or a boundary is reached.
trap: Do not compare marginal utility alone when prices differ.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: The next notebook yields 18 units of utility and costs 3. The next pen yields 10 units and costs 2. Notebook utility per dollar is 6; pen utility per dollar is 5. At this margin, shifting some spending toward notebooks improves utility until the ratios converge or a boundary is reached. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Demand, supply and equilibrium shifts
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Demand and supply relate a good’s own price to quantities, holding other determinants fixed. A change in that price moves along a curve. Income, preferences, input costs and technology can instead shift curves. Equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A shortage places upward pressure on price; a surplus places downward pressure. If both curves shift, one equilibrium change may be ambiguous without information about shift magnitudes.
formula: Equilibrium: Qd = Qs; surplus = Qs − Qd
steps: Let demand be P = 100 − Q and supply be P = 20 + Q.
Then 2Q = 80, so Q = 40 and P = 60.
An increase in demand shifts demand right; with supply unchanged, both equilibrium price and quantity rise.
trap: An increase in quantity demanded from a lower own price is not a rightward demand shift.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Let demand be P = 100 − Q and supply be P = 20 + Q. Set 100 − Q = 20 + Q. Then 2Q = 80, so Q = 40 and P = 60. An increase in demand shifts demand right; with supply unchanged, both equilibrium price and quantity rise. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: An increase in quantity demanded from a lower own price is not a rightward demand shift.

title: Elasticity and revenue
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Elasticity measures percentage responsiveness rather than slope in units. Price elasticity of demand is usually reported as an absolute value; values above one are elastic. When demand is elastic, a price increase reduces total revenue, holding demand fixed. Supply elasticity depends in part on adjustment time. Positive income elasticity identifies a normal good; negative income elasticity an inferior good. Positive cross-price elasticity suggests substitutes, while a negative value suggests complements.
formula: Midpoint elasticity = |(ΔQ / average Q) / (ΔP / average P)|; TR = P × Q
steps: Price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80.
Quantity changes by −20 / 90; price changes by 2 / 11.
The absolute elasticity is about 1.22, so demand is elastic over the interval.
Revenue falls from 1000 to 960, consistent with the elastic classification.
trap: A steep curve is not automatically inelastic at every point; elasticity uses percentages.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Quantity changes by −20 / 90; price changes by 2 / 11. The absolute elasticity is about 1.22, so demand is elastic over the interval. Revenue falls from 1000 to 960, consistent with the elastic classification. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.prompt: A positive cross-price elasticity between two goods indicates what relationship?
options: Substitutes.

Both have perfectly elastic supply.
questions.hint: A steep curve is not automatically inelastic at every point; elasticity uses percentages.

title: Taxes, ceilings and market surplus
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A binding price ceiling lies below equilibrium and creates a shortage in the basic competitive model. A binding floor lies above equilibrium and creates a surplus. A per-unit tax creates a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive. The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden, regardless of which side remits it. Lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss; tax revenue itself is a transfer, not all deadweight loss.
formula: Tax wedge = buyer price − seller price; DWL = ½ × tax × reduction in Q for linear curves
steps: A competitive market initially trades 50 units.
A tax of 4 per unit reduces trade to 40.
Tax revenue is 4 × 40 = 160.
The triangular lost surplus is ½ × 4 × 10 = 20 under linear curves without externalities.
trap: Who legally pays the tax does not by itself determine its economic incidence.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A competitive market initially trades 50 units. A tax of 4 per unit reduces trade to 40. Tax revenue is 4 × 40 = 160. The triangular lost surplus is ½ × 4 × 10 = 20 under linear curves without externalities. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: World prices, imports and tariffs
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A small price-taking country facing a world price below its closed-economy equilibrium imports the difference between domestic demand and supply. Consumers gain from the lower price while domestic producers lose; total surplus rises in the basic model. A tariff raises the domestic price when it does not eliminate imports. It transfers some surplus to domestic producers and government while creating production and consumption distortions.
formula: Imports = domestic Qd − domestic Qs at the domestic price
steps: At the world price, domestic buyers want 90 units and domestic firms supply 30.
Imports are 60 units.
A tariff raises domestic price; demand falls to 80 and supply rises to 40.
Imports fall to 40; the tariff reduces some gains from trade under the small-country assumptions.
trap: A tariff does not make imports rise merely because government receives revenue.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: At the world price, domestic buyers want 90 units and domestic firms supply 30. Imports are 60 units. A tariff raises domestic price; demand falls to 80 and supply rises to 40. Imports fall to 40; the tariff reduces some gains from trade under the small-country assumptions. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

part: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
title: Production and short-run costs
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: In the short run at least one input is fixed. Marginal product is the extra output from an additional variable input. Diminishing marginal returns means marginal product eventually falls as more variable input works with fixed inputs; total output can still rise. Fixed cost does not vary with output. Marginal cost is the extra total cost per additional output and rises when marginal product falls, if the variable input price is constant.
formula: TC = FC + VC; ATC = TC / Q; MC = ΔTC / ΔQ
steps: A firm’s fixed cost is 60 and variable cost is 140 when output is 20.
Total cost is 200; average total cost is 10.
At 21 units, total cost is 212.
The 21st unit has marginal cost 12, above current ATC, so it pulls ATC upward.
trap: Falling marginal product is not the same as negative marginal product.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A firm’s fixed cost is 60 and variable cost is 140 when output is 20. Total cost is 200; average total cost is 10. At 21 units, total cost is 212. The 21st unit has marginal cost 12, above current ATC, so it pulls ATC upward. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

options: ATC falls as output expands.

Fixed cost increases.
Total cost is zero.
questions.hint: Falling marginal product is not the same as negative marginal product.

part: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
title: Scale and the meaning of profit
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: In the long run all inputs can vary. Economies of scale mean long-run average total cost falls as output increases; diseconomies mean it rises. Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs from revenue. Economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs, including the owner’s forgone wage or return. Zero economic profit includes a normal return to the owner and does not imply that revenue or accounting profit is zero.
formula: Economic profit = revenue − explicit costs − implicit costs
steps: Annual revenue is 200, explicit costs are 140 and the owner forgoes a job paying 40.
Accounting profit is 200 − 140 = 60.
Economic profit is 200 − 140 − 40 = 20.
If implicit costs rose to 60 with everything else unchanged, economic profit would become zero.
trap: Normal profit is an opportunity cost included in economic cost.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Annual revenue is 200, explicit costs are 140 and the owner forgoes a job paying 40. Accounting profit is 200 − 140 = 60. Economic profit is 200 − 140 − 40 = 20. If implicit costs rose to 60 with everything else unchanged, economic profit would become zero. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Normal profit is an opportunity cost included in economic cost.

part: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
title: Choosing output and deciding whether to shut down
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A firm chooses output by comparing marginal revenue and marginal cost, with profit maximization where MR = MC on the relevant rising-MC portion in the continuous model. A competitive firm takes price as given, so MR = P. In the short run it produces if revenue covers variable cost at the best output; otherwise shutting down loses only fixed cost. Long-run exit depends on covering all economic costs.
formula: Competitive firm: P = MR; produce in short run when P ≥ minimum AVC
steps: A competitive firm can sell 10 units at price 8.
At that output, AVC is 6 and ATC is 10; assume it is the profit-maximizing operating output.
Revenue is 80 and total cost is 100, so the firm loses 20 if it operates.
Variable cost is 60 and fixed cost is 40; operating loses less than shutting down, which loses 40.
trap: A loss does not automatically imply immediate shutdown.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A competitive firm can sell 10 units at price 8. At that output, AVC is 6 and ATC is 10; assume it is the profit-maximizing operating output. Revenue is 80 and total cost is 100, so the firm loses 20 if it operates. Variable cost is 60 and fixed cost is 40; operating loses less than shutting down, which loses 40. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: A loss does not automatically imply immediate shutdown.

part: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
title: Competitive adjustment and efficiency
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A perfectly competitive market has many price-taking firms, a standardized product and free entry and exit. Short-run economic profit attracts entry, shifting market supply right and lowering price. In a constant-cost industry, the long-run competitive outcome has zero economic profit and production at minimum ATC. With no externalities or other failures, P = MC supports allocative efficiency; minimum ATC supports productive efficiency.
formula: Long-run competitive benchmark: P = MC = minimum ATC
steps: Firms initially earn positive economic profit.
Entry adds market supply.
The market price falls, reducing each firm’s economic profit.
In the long-run benchmark, entry stops when economic profit is zero; price equals minimum ATC.
trap: Zero long-run economic profit does not mean no incentive to remain in business.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Firms initially earn positive economic profit. Entry adds market supply. The market price falls, reducing each firm’s economic profit. In the long-run benchmark, entry stops when economic profit is zero; price equals minimum ATC. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

options: A legal monopoly automatically.
Entry and a rightward market supply shift.
Exit and a leftward supply shift.
A permanent rise in each firm’s demand.
questions.hint: Zero long-run economic profit does not mean no incentive to remain in business.
questions.explain: Entry and a rightward market supply shift.

questions.hint: Identify the units and substitute into the relationship above. Enter a number or fraction without unit symbols.

title: Market power and monopoly decisions
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Market power lets a firm influence its selling price. A single-price monopolist faces the market demand curve, so selling another unit generally requires lowering the price on earlier units; MR lies below demand. It selects quantity where MR = MC and then reads price from demand. Barriers to entry can sustain economic profit, but monopoly does not guarantee profit. Relative to the efficient competitive benchmark, monopoly restricts output when price exceeds marginal cost.
formula: Choose Q where MR = MC; read P from demand; profit = (P − ATC)Q
steps: Demand is P = 100 − Q and MR = 100 − 2Q.
With constant MC = 20, solve 100 − 2Q = 20 to get Q = 40.
Read price from demand: P = 60.
With ATC = 30 at that output, profit is (60 − 30) × 40 = 1200.
trap: Do not read the monopoly selling price from the MR curve.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Demand is P = 100 − Q and MR = 100 − 2Q. With constant MC = 20, solve 100 − 2Q = 20 to get Q = 40. Read price from demand: P = 60. With ATC = 30 at that output, profit is (60 − 30) × 40 = 1200. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

At the competitive quantity regardless of demand.
On its demand curve at the chosen quantity.
questions.hint: Do not read the monopoly selling price from the MR curve.
questions.explain: On its demand curve at the chosen quantity.

title: Price discrimination and differentiated sellers
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Price discrimination charges different prices for reasons beyond cost differences and requires market power, separation of buyers and limits on resale. Perfect price discrimination can capture consumer surplus and expand output to the efficient quantity in the simple no-externality model. Monopolistic competition instead combines differentiated products with entry. Entry can eliminate long-run economic profit while firms still charge above marginal cost and operate with excess capacity.
formula: Monopolistic competition in long run: P = ATC, typically P > MC
steps: A differentiated seller charges 15 and produces 20 units.
ATC at that output is also 15, so economic profit is zero.
MC is 9, so the firm still has a markup of 6.
Free entry can remove profit without turning its downward-sloping demand into a horizontal curve.
trap: Zero profit alone does not prove allocative efficiency.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A differentiated seller charges 15 and produces 20 units. ATC at that output is also 15, so economic profit is zero. MC is 9, so the firm still has a markup of 6. Free entry can remove profit without turning its downward-sloping demand into a horizontal curve. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Strategic choices and Nash equilibrium
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: An oligopoly has few interdependent firms: one firm’s best action depends on rivals’ behavior. A dominant strategy is best regardless of what the other player does. A Nash equilibrium is a set of actions in which neither player gains by changing alone, given the other’s action. Collusion may raise joint profit but create an incentive to deviate. A one-shot model does not by itself predict every repeated interaction.
formula: Best response: compare your own payoff while holding the other player’s action fixed
steps: Two firms each choose a high or low price.
High/high pays each 8; low/high pays the low-price firm 10 and its rival 2; low/low pays each 4.
Low is better whether the rival chooses high (10 > 8) or low (4 > 2).
Low/low is the dominant-strategy Nash equilibrium even though high/high gives higher joint profit.
trap: Joint-profit maximization is not automatically a Nash equilibrium.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Two firms each choose a high or low price. High/high pays each 8; low/high pays the low-price firm 10 and its rival 2; low/low pays each 4. Low is better whether the rival chooses high (10 > 8) or low (4 > 2). Low/low is the dominant-strategy Nash equilibrium even though high/high gives higher joint profit. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Joint-profit maximization is not automatically a Nash equilibrium.
questions.explain: No player gains from changing alone given the others’ actions.

title: Regulating a natural monopoly
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A natural monopoly can supply the relevant market at lower cost as one firm because average cost declines over that output range. Setting price equal to MC achieves the no-externality allocative benchmark but may leave revenue below total cost. Average-cost pricing can allow the firm to cover economic cost while producing more than an unregulated monopolist, though less than the efficient output. Policy comparisons require explicit cost and demand assumptions.
formula: Break-even regulation: P = ATC; efficient price benchmark: P = MC
steps: At the efficient output of 100 units, MC is 4 and ATC is 7.
A price of 4 creates revenue of 400.
Total cost is 700, leaving a loss of 300.
A subsidy of 300 would cover that loss in this numerical example; financing and incentives require separate evaluation.
trap: Marginal-cost pricing need not let a natural monopoly break even.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: At the efficient output of 100 units, MC is 4 and ATC is 7. A price of 4 creates revenue of 400. Total cost is 700, leaving a loss of 300. A subsidy of 300 would cover that loss in this numerical example; financing and incentives require separate evaluation. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Derived demand for labor
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Demand for an input is derived from demand for its output. Marginal revenue product is the extra revenue from hiring one more unit of the input. In a competitive output market, MRP equals marginal product times output price. Diminishing marginal product can make labor demand slope downward. A firm hires additional workers while their marginal revenue product covers their marginal factor cost, rather than comparing wages with total revenue.
formula: MRP = MP × MR; competitive output market: MRP = MP × P
steps: An additional worker produces 6 units and the product sells competitively at 5.
The worker adds revenue of 30.
If the wage and marginal factor cost are 24, hiring that worker adds 6 to profit before any other changing costs.

title: Shifts in input demand and supply
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Product demand, worker productivity and the prices of related inputs can shift labor demand. Population, preferences, migration and alternative opportunities can shift labor supply. A wage change moves along existing curves; it does not by itself shift them. Higher productivity can increase demand for labor, but substitution and output effects can interact when another input becomes cheaper. State which effect the problem assumes dominates.

title: Competitive hiring and marginal factor cost
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A firm hiring in a perfectly competitive factor market takes the wage as given. Its marginal factor cost is the wage, so it hires to the point where MRP equals the wage in the continuous model. With discrete workers, hire those whose added revenue is at least their added cost. A firm may face competition in the labor market while having market power in its output market; then MRP uses marginal revenue, not the product price.

steps: Successive workers have MRP values of 50, 40, 30 and 20.

Hire three workers, assuming these are all relevant variable costs.

title: Monopsony and a carefully set wage floor
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A monopsonist has buying power in a factor market. In the simple uniform-wage model it faces upward-sloping labor supply: to attract another worker it raises the wage for all workers. Marginal factor cost therefore exceeds the wage. It selects labor where MRP = MFC and reads the wage from labor supply. A moderate minimum wage can raise both wages and employment in this model, but an excessively high floor can reduce employment.

part: Market Failure and the Role of Government
title: External costs and efficient output
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A negative externality imposes costs on others that private decision-makers do not fully bear. Marginal social cost equals marginal private cost plus marginal external cost. Without correction, a competitive market can produce too much when private benefits equal social benefits but private cost understates social cost. A corrective tax equal to marginal external damage at the efficient quantity aligns marginal incentives in the basic model.

steps: At a quantity, private marginal cost is 12 and external marginal damage is 5.

trap: The efficient target is not automatically zero pollution.

part: Market Failure and the Role of Government
title: Public goods and common resources
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A public good is nonrival and nonexcludable: one person’s use does not reduce another’s and excluding nonpayers is difficult. Free riding can cause private underprovision. A common resource is rival but difficult to exclude people from using, so individual incentives can lead to overuse. For a public good, marginal willingness to pay is added vertically across people for the same quantity; private goods instead add quantities at a given price.
formula: Public-good MSB at Q = sum of individuals’ marginal benefits at that Q
steps: At one extra unit of a public warning service, A values it at 8 and B at 5.
Because they enjoy the same unit, add their marginal benefits: 13.
If marginal cost is 10, the unit’s total benefit exceeds its cost.

title: Choosing and evaluating interventions

idea: Taxes, subsidies, quantity limits, tradable permits and regulation change incentives in different ways. title: Inequality, income and redistribution
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: An income distribution describes how total income is divided across people or households. A Lorenz curve plots cumulative population shares against cumulative income shares; a curve farther below equality generally indicates more unequal distribution. Poverty and inequality are different concepts. Taxes and transfers can change disposable-income distribution, while evaluation also considers incentives, administrative costs and the choice of comparison group. Correlation between characteristics and income does not by itself identify a cause.
